subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF 12 MILE FISHING ZONE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF 12 MILE FISHING ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house on the law of the sea, a subject of considerable importance in international affairs and of particular significance for Canada, the seventh largest fishing nation in the world and the fourth largest trading nation, possessing the world's longest coastlines.
Traditionally the breadth of the territorial sea has been three nautical miles, but the Canadian view has long been that a breadth of three miles is not adequate for all purposes. It was on December 7, 1956 that a Canadian representative put forward at a meeting of the sixth committee of the United Nations the proposal, which later came to be known at Geneva as the Canadian proposal, of a contiguous fishing zone beyond the three mile territorial sea which would extend to a limit of 12 miles.
In the light of the failure of efforts to bring about an agreement on the breadth of the territorial sea and the contiguous fishing zone, the government has decided, after careful deliberation, that the time has come to take firm action to protect Canada's fishing industry. It is well known that foreign fishing operations off Canada's east coast, which have increased enormously over the past five years, are not only depleting our offshore fisheries resources but are posing other problems. There are indications also that Canada's west coast fisheries may soon be threatened. In similar circumstances an increasing number of countries have felt themselves compelled to abandon the three mile fishing limit. All told, more than 40 countries have already extended their territorial limits, and more than 50 countries their fisheries limits beyond three miles.
With these considerations in mind the Canadian government has decided to establish a 12 mile exclusive fisheries zone along the whole of Canada's coastline as of mid-May, 1964, and to implement the straight base line
system at the same time as the basis from which Canada's territorial sea and exclusive fisheries zone shall be measured.
The government recognizes that such action will necessarily have implications for other countries, particularly the United States of America and France, both of which have treaty fishing rights in some of the areas affected and claims to "historic" fishing rights in other areas in question. In the case of Canada and the U.S.A. in particular, there is a long tradition of friendly and fruitful co-operation on fisheries problems, and any action by Canada on these matters will, as in the past, take full account of United States interests, as well as of those other countries affected.
It may be recalled that in my discussions with President Kennedy at Hyannis Port I informed him that the Canadian government would shortly be taking decisions to establish a 12 mile fishing zone. The President reserved the longstanding American position in support of the three mile limit. He also called attention to the "historic" and treaty fishing rights of the U.S.A., and I assured him that these rights would be taken into account. Discussions will be held with the United States with a view to determining the nature and extent of the U.S.A. rights and interests which may be affected by the action which Canada is taking. Discussions will also be opened as soon as possible with other countries affected, and it is our hope and belief that we will be able to reach agreement with such countries on mutually satisfactory arrangements.

This might be a convenient time, Mr. Speaker, to reply to a question which was asked me on May 28 by the hon. member for Queens. subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my race against the clock last Thursday, I lost, and so I was unable to complete the short speech I had begun to make in respect to the establishment of a committee on defence.
However, I am glad that an occasion is given me today, following the death of His Holiness Pope John XXIII, to pay a public tribute to that great man for the important part he played in favour of world peace.
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat what I said the other night to the effect that this debate on the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) aiming at the establishment of a special committee on defence is not a debate on defence itself. The hon. members who preceded me have inadvertently explained the policies of their parties, when they should have made constructive suggestions for the proper operation of the committee.
If we read again the resolution on the order paper, we see that the purpose of the committee isto report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, if the defence committee is not given greater powers, it is useless to set it up because then it would be just a make-believe body, one that would have in fact no real power.
That committee should be in a position to impose its decisions on the government because if we go to the trouble of setting up a committee to study defence problems, we must, to be logical, give it some authority.

Social Credit pledges that upon election, it will immediately appoint a non-partisan parliamentary defence committee through recommending defence policies in light of secret security information, military requirements, and international developments. Since the question was raised as to whether Canada should get nuclear weapons, we have realized that Canada has been subject to pressures from many sources, and in the past, those pressures have placed our country in the rather unusual situation which we have experienced in the last parliament when nobody seemed to know exactly what was our position concerning defence problems.
On the one hand, we are under American influence and our friends, the Liberals, should know something about that. This influence is being shown more and more openly.
Mr. Speaker, if you would read a recent article written by Mr. Melvin Conant in the International Journal magazine, you would find revealing facts such as these:

For it is certain that other weapon systems, now anticipated, and of the nuclear variety, will deepen and enlarge the Canadian commitment.

In the same article, Mr. Speaker, we read the following passage:

If all the above suggest the historic importance of the initial decision which Canada will make this


spring, then perhaps some fresh perspective is gained on the nature of that decision. Canadians are not being asked to determine simply the arming of several contemporary weapons systems; Canadians have been asked to say if they intend to be a major participant in the alliance. Its friends can only hope it 'will answer the question with a ringing affirmative.
(Translation):
On that point, Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that the United States are determined to have Canada equipped with nuclear arms, so that we would, in a way, pay our share of the expenses. Moreover, the United States would thus feel secure in the knowledge that we would integrate into their defence policy, and would not, if war broke out, suddenly decide to stay neutral.
If we continue to acquire nuclear arms as we did under the Liberals, we shall play straight into the hands of our American neighbours.
But we must also take into account the influence from the east, that is to say from the communist world. That influence shows itself in many ways, through the Canadian peace congress, the voice of women and other similar groups which are convinced that Canada can do without nuclear arms.
Let us not fall into that trap either, Mr. Speaker. I believe we should see clearly the purpose of the influences that are being exerted from both sides.
I have here a publication issued by the national committee of the communist party of Canada dated May 16. We can see in it the relations which exist at present between the communist party of Canada, influenced by the communist party from Moscow, and a certain organization such as the national congress for peace. Here is what we actually find in the statement of the national communist party:
The will of the people must prevail. On April 8, 59 per cent of the electorate repudiated the Liberals.
It is certain that the Liberal party does not have the authority at this time to acquire nuclear weapons for Canada. This is what we find, in terms quite similar, in a publication sent to the NATO council which met here in Ottawa in May 1963:
(Text):
The Liberal government, which took office with a minority of seats, has no mandate from the Canadian people to enter into any arrangement or treaty involving nuclear arms for Canada.
(Translation):
We can perceive in the same publication the influence from the U.S.S.R. which is obvious in the following words:
(Text):
Formation of a military alliance of the west has inevitably produced a military alliance of "the east".

(Translation):
Then one can see in reading those letters how deceitful is the propaganda of that movement which claims to be a movement for peace because the west is charged with the fault of the east which wanted to get armed the same as all the other countries.
Mr. Speaker, I think that a committee where the matter of defence would be discussed is the most natural system which we can dream of in order to protect ourselves against all those influences bringing us to take nonCanadian stands, for they are rather American or Russian, depending on whether or not we accept nuclear arms.
I am not one of those who are automatically opposed to nuclear arms, nor am I one of those who will necessarily accept them.
I am of the opinion of a certain Mr. Tos-sanyi, a professional engineer and geologist, commanding officer of the Hungarian paratroopers regiment, who has examined the question seriously and has come to the conclusion that we should not have nuclear weapons. However, I would not say that I am entirely of his opinion when he says that we should not have nuclear weapons of any kind whatsoever. It is logical and reasonable to think, in view of our geographic position, that we could come to the conclusion that defensive weapons are a necessity.
I will quote what this gentleman has to say about the influences which come from all sides and which affect our judgment: (Text):
According to Time magazine, in 1959, Norstad, the allied supreme commander in Europe, briefed the Canadian cabinet in Ottawa on NATO's changing needs, and suggested that Canada should switch from an interceptor role to a strike-reconnaissance role, and suggested the two-key control. Subsequently the so-called "tactical strike-reconnaissance" aircraft, the CF-104, was acquired-
From utterances, it appears that our political leaders were under the impression that with the acquisition of these weapons, we still had a nonnuclear alternative.
(Translation):
The funny part of the situation, Mr. Speaker, is to see our government leaders who have been squabbling for a certain time to determine whether or not there has actually been any commitments.
A Toronto newspaperman working for the Daily Star has given a good summary of the situation when he said: "In fact, there has been no formal commitment", but he adds in conclusion:
(Text):
If the Pearson government is convinced we should get nuclear arms, let it justify the weapons on their merit, if any. But let it stop trying to tell the Canadian people it's all the fault of the Diefenbaker administration.
Appointment of Defence Committee (Translation):
The situation continues because nobody seems to know whether there has been any commitment.
Indeed, the Diefenbaker government was overthrown because it refused to tell us whether there were any commitments and because it had no defence policy in spite of the representations we made in that connection.
Today we find ourselves in exactly the same situation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it would be up to the parliamentary committee to determine how much we are bound by any commitment and, if there is no commitment at all, to take a decision which would be truly our own. It would be a "made in Canada" decision not a "made in Russia" or a "made in U.S.A." decision.
Mr. Tossanyi continues as follows: (Text):
One cannot escape the conviction that Canada was gradually accepting nuclear armament through the back door, which suited perfectly the U.S. and Canadian military planning.
(Translation):
In my opinion, sir, it is just as bad for Canada's defence policy to follow too closely that of the United States as it would be to follow that of Russia.
Canada is an adult nation and I feel that, as such, it should adopt a truly Canadian policy.
That is why I find that it was ill-advised on the part of Judge Thorson of the exchequer court to make the remarks he made. In my opinion, it is ill-advised for any man holding such a high position in our country to try to influence the policy of the government and the decisions that might be taken by the defence committee at this time. It is up to the parliamentary committee on defence to establish our defence policy.
Comments from outsiders such as Judge Thorson are ill-advised and ill-timed.
Consequently, in view of the complex decisions we will have to make concerning defence problems, I feel that Canada has a unique opportunity at this time to play an intelligent role toward the achievement of world peace.
We are placed between two spheres of influence, each trying to get Canada to accept a foreign-made policy.
In my opinion, the main purpose of the special committee on defence will be to see to it that Canada plays its role between these two spheres of influence and decide where it should stand better to serve peace.

Appointment of Defence Committee (Text):
Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple
Creek): Speaking on this motion, Mr. Speaker, may I first state that I was sorry the government found it necessary to restrict the membership of this committee to 24. To me it is fairly obvious there are a great many more hon. members of the house who are extremely interested in the subject of defence and who are obviously not all of the same opinion.
Those of us who are not selected as members of the committee will be restricted in our efforts to study the issue as we would like to do. We will be unable to obtain answers to the questions which as individuals we have a right to ask, and also to ask on behalf of the people we represent. When the Prime Minister remarked that this was an entirely new type of committee to be set up, the first one in Canada, I hoped he would have made the committee unrestricted and open to all hon. members of the house, to all those who are interested, and this would have given the privilege to all hon. members to ask questions as they desired.
As the motion now reads, only 24 selected members will have this privilege. I am aware that hon. members of the house can attend the committee hearings, if they wish, but they are restricted in asking questions.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of National Defence state that the purpose of the committee is to study all aspects of defence, including policy. He felt all hon. members should be given every opportunity to obtain first hand information on the facts. I appreciate that. As recorded at page 485 of Hansard for May 30 the minister said:
-notwithstanding the terrible confusion which engulfed most aspects of this question during the campaign, and notwithstanding the confusion which still exists and the great mass of inaccurate and incomplete information, we think there is a genuine desire on the part of all hon. members to come to grips with this subject-
I believe he could have added that there is also a great desire on the part of the public to have the facts placed before them, after the confusion we all know existed during the recent election campaign.
In view of the minister's statement I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to get the committee off to a good start by placing one important fact before the house this time. To begin with, I am sure the Canadian people would be very grateful to him for a direct answer, yes or no, to a question put to him on May 20, as recorded at page 37 of Hansard of that date, and which he left unanswered. I would put the question again:
In an interview shortly after being sworn in the present minister is reported to have said that he expected a Canada-United States agreement on custody and control of nuclear warheads to be signed in about a month's time, an agreement

which requires both parliamentary ratification and congressional approval as well as the signatures of the contracting parties.
In view of this statement, would the minister now refute his former claim, which misled the Canadian public, that the Conservative government had fully committed Canada to equipping its air squadrons and Bomarc missiles with nuclear warheads-
And the rest of the question read:
_and was therefore abandoning its duty in not
accepting them.
As the minister declined to answer, may I ask him how can he relate what he told the public during the election campaign, about Canada's commitment on defence, to the statement he made in the House of Commons in reply to a question put to him by the house leader of the opposition? The question, as recorded at page 484 of Hansard of May 30 was:
May I ask the minister what agreement has to be signed?
His reply was:
As the hon. gentleman should know, if he had done his homework on these matters, these warheads cannot be made available to any friendly nation unless, first, a general agreement has been signed between that nation and the United States of America; and as my hon. friend further knows, his government spent about four years trying to work out such an agreement. With the speed with which they did things they still have not achieved it.
I will take the minister's reply, which is now recorded in Hansard, as the word of a responsible member of the government; that when the Liberals took office in April, 1963 there was no signed agreement and therefore no commitment by Canada to acquire nuclear warheads. I believe the present government, and particularly the Minister of National Defence, are now duty bound to inform the Canadian public of the truth that upon taking office they did find that Canada had not been officially committed. As late as April 8, 1963 Canada had not signed any agreement to take nuclear warheads for her weapons. Therefore there was no commitment on any one's part.
I further believe it is the duty of the press to inform the Canadian people that while the Conservative government was in power no commitment had been made to accept nuclear warheads by Canada. At least let the committee begin with clarification on this one point, a point which confused the public during the election campaign. There were no grounds for the Liberal accusations at that time, and I think it has been established by the minister's statement that Canada was definitely not committed when the Conservative government was in power.

speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Actually, Mr. Speaker, the cost of defence has always been a staggering item to all taxpayers and I, as well as a great number of other taxpayers, do not

believe we are getting our money's worth. I believe we all accept the fact that funds are expended today for certain equipment which may be outmoded tomorrow. But it is not equipment I intend to deal with at the present time. When dealing with defence, I feel the public are entitled to straightforward answers to some pertinent questions, one of which might be: are the three services which make up our forces of national defence organized to fight in accordance with the present day concept of war? My answer to that question would be, no. I understand our military organization has changed little since the days of 1914 or 1940 although the role of our forces today is entirely different from what it was then. Our whole organization is based on a five and six division operation, including the numerous headquarters staffs which go to maintain units within those divisions. Our military organization is top heavy; it should be modernized and streamlined in keeping with Canada's new role in the defence of the North American continent. If the trend to expand the senior positions in our services could be curtailed, the taxpayer, I believe, could be saved a considerable amount of money.
On the subject of organization and senior personnel, may I say that I believe we have delegated, since 1950, too much power to the chief of our general staff. When the National Defence Act was revised in 1950, personal authority was given to the C.G.S. far beyond that of his counterpart in Great Britain. British parliamentary reforms throughout the years established the principle that no single commander in chief should have sole responsibility for the control and administration of the army. Ever since 1904, since the Esher reforms, the British army has been administered by an army council composed of political, military and civil service officials. This council has survived severe tests in two world wars and has remained an effective and efficient instrument of government policy in the administration of the army.
The weakness of full military control similar to that which is at present in effect in Canada has been illustrated over and over again in other countries. History reveals that the German general staff was supreme in military matters and powerful enough to ignore the advice of the civil authorities. As a result, decisions of the German general staff plunged Germany into two needless and unsuccessful wars. Surely, no similar action should be taken in Canada delegating authority to the military. It should be a warning to us in Canada; we do not want to follow the same pattern as Germany did.

Appointment of Defence Committee
One of the pitfalls resulting from the power delegated to the chief of staff by the Canadian parliament is the natural tendency of people in authority to gather about them like-thinking friends. Someone has said: "Where everyone thinks alike, no one thinks at all". This situation, to me, represents a major danger attaching to this type of control. I understand that the chief of the general staff is also a member of the joint chiefs of staff committee but that he is not bound by the decisions of that committee. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) told us the other day that the chairman of this committee could be called as a witness before the committee which we are now proposing to set up. But if the chief of the general staff is not bound by the decisions of the joint chiefs of staff committee, what would be the use of calling the chairman of that committee to give evidence? Regardless of the confidence we have in our present chief of staff or in his successors, I submit that such delegation of power to one individual is dangerous, not only to Canada but also to the individual who is charged with this responsibility. I trust the present minister will introduce legislation to rectify the existing outmoded system of military organization and control.
Another question which might be raised is this: are our services equipped to fight on a nuclear battlefield? This is a question which should be answered to the satisfaction of hon. members of this house. It brings up the contentious subject of equipping our armed forces with nuclear weapons. Some will argue that if such a step were taken we should be joining the nuclear family. As members of this house, let us not fool ourselves. We are charter members of that family now. We have been an exporter of uranium for the past 14 or 15 years and as such have been full members of a great nuclear alliance whether we like it or not. Even if we wished, now, to proclaim our innocence in this regard it would be too late. We cannot deny the fact that Canada has supplied essential material for the manufacture of nuclear explosives, nor can we plead innocence by saying we were unaware of the use to which our raw material was being put. If guilt is to be attached to any one person, let us face the facts. We are all guilty.
Hardly a week passes in which members of this house do not receive a brief or letters from some organization maintaining that if we were to acquire nuclear weapons we would end all possible chances of bringing peace to the world. Other correspondents maintain we should disarm in order to bring peace to the world. Still others maintain that if we were to ban the bomb we should

Appointment of Defence Committee bring peace to the world. In each case, it would seem to me, those subscribing to any of these theories assume they have a monopoly on the desire for peace, and all others subscribing to contrary ideas or views are classed as warmongers. In some cases, I would suggest, certain individuals have lost sight of the main objective, which is one of peace, and have gone overboard as to their professed method of obtaining this objective. The desire for peace is, I believe, the sincere desire of everyone in this house and of every Canadian, even if we cannot agree on the method of achieving this objective. The desire for peace is not confined to any one individual, or group of individuals, nor does it necessarily follow that any one party or individual has the solution to this problem. Like many others, I believe Canada should acquire nuclear arms and that by so doing we would best ensure that our efforts to bring peace to this modem world will be successful.
The question of whether these arms would be defensive or offensive weapons is, to me, splitting hairs. Any weapon can be a defensive or an offensive weapon depending on how it is used. It also depends on the range of the weapon.
To those who maintain the acquisition of nuclear arms by Canada would be detrimental to world disarmament, I say: let us be realistic. In my opinion, it is not logical to assume that the U.S.S.R. are really interested in general disarmament. Communism was born in violence, and its spread to other countries has always been accompanied at some stage with force or threat of force, and has been maintained by the same means. For Russia to disarm would mean the end of its avowed aim of world domination and, certainly, the loss of its satellite states. The Soviet union would no longer be a world power.
I believe the fact that the free world possesses a nuclear striking force capable of dealing unacceptable damage to any aggressor has prevented the proponents of communism from embarking on an adventure designed to force the free world to submit to their principles. I suggest that the creation of the NATO shield saved Europe and the free world from Soviet occupation and further aggression. Our duty, I believe, is to convince the Soviet union that their might is cancelled out by the strength of our defences-I refer to the defences of the North American continent under NORAD. The power of the free world to retaliate is the greatest deterrent to any thought Russia may have of world domination.
As a sovereign nation, we should be proud to be an ally in the free world, playing our part in an undertaking which has halted the

advance of the aggressor. Some in this house have contended that Canada should adopt a neutral role. They have pointed out the advantages which have accrued to countries such as Switzerland and Sweden as a result of their neutrality. Very seldom is mention made of the disadvantages encountered by Holland and Belgium because of their adoption of a like role. History has proven that there are no advantages to countries in a neutral role if the potential aggressor will not recognize or respect that neutrality. The geographical location of a country in a conventional war dictated whether or not the country would benefit from a neutral role. Geographical location will mean very little of a practical nature in an atomic war.
As a member of parliament I believe, as I am sure we all believe, that it is our responsibility to legislate for the best defence the people can afford. Where can we get the most for our defence dollars? As I previously stated we are not unanimous as to the method of providing this defence. I support the acquisition of nuclear warheads for Canadian defence because I believe they will reduce the amount of fallout from a number of atomic bombs, should they be released over Canada by manned bombers or otherwise. I also suggest that we obtain nuclear warheads for every weapon we have capable of firing them. Because if my information is correct, that nuclear warheads are the only known method of preventing fallout from atomic bombs, then it is our duty to prevent as much fallout as we can from taking place over Canadian soil. We should place more emphasis on the fallout from the atomic bomb, not on the bomb itself. Fallout is the more dangerous to our people.
Most Canadians believe the United States is determined to defend the North American continent-and in so doing they are bound to defend Canada from external aggression, almost regardless of whether or not Canadians wish to be defended.
If this is the present defensive plan of the United States, then does it not follow that Canada can never, consistent with her own interests, ignore the requirements of American security? Because in continental defence, which I think we have to admit is what is required at the present time, we recognize that the security of the United States is also the security of Canada. A joint defence is essential because of the changed circumstances. We cannot defend ourselves alone.

Mr. Speaker, I am, like everyone else, is or should be, keenly interested in this matter of defence. If I might be a little sentimental to start, may I say that I am interested in this question of defence because I am a

member of humanity. I am one of the billions which go to make up this world. I also have the honour of being one of the 265 members of the House of Commons representing the 18 million souls who reside in our country. Going beyond that, I have the honour of being the representative of the wonderful constituency of Vancouver East. And going beyond that, I have a wife, three children, and the three children have given me 12 grandchildren. So that going from the individual to the family, to the community, to the constituency, to the province, to the country and to the world, we must all have a keen interest in defence, and in the meaning of defence, so that there shall never be another world war. Because on an individual, a family, a community and a world basis we want to see ourselves, our families, our countrymen and our people live their lives to a natural death, not to an unnatural death through the holocaust of a thermonuclear suicidal war. That, sir, is my introduction, because it is the way I feel.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to repeat the broad principles and policy in defence and foreign affairs as we in the New Democratic party see them because they have been very fully and capably outlined by our leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). I have no hesitation in saying that I think one of the curses of this parliament and of previous parliaments is too much useless repetition, and so I do not intend to be guilty of that. In the time at my disposal I want to refer to the resolution before us, which is concerned with the appointment of a special committee of the House of Commons on defence. I am most certainly in support of the appointment of that committee. I am most certainly in favour of the broadest possible terms of reference. I hope it will be a committee that can function. Committees can function if they are given the opportunity. You need only refer to the public accounts committee of past sessions to see that it did function. It did work and it brought in recommendations; and if cabinet ministers and the departments concerned did not pay any attention to those recommendations, then the next year the public accounts committee called them to account. So that committees can function.
Mr. Speaker, I hope this proposed committee will function, but I am sorry to say that I am wondering whether it will. That is why I am speaking this afternoon. I had the privilege of being a member of the prior committee on defence established in 1960. I hold in my hand the transcript of the evidence of that committee. It is quite a blue book. It was a committee appointed by the previous government. At the moment I am interested 28902-5-41J

Appointment of Defence Committee in two members of that 1960 committee- myself, who was the sole representative from our party on that committee, and from the former opposition, the hon. member for the constituency of Trinity, now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).
Mr. Speaker, if I may say so, between the two of us we might have been called the "unholy trinity" on that committee because neither of us ever missed a meeting. It was just about as close as we ever came to coalition because we always sat side by side, and if he could not get a seconder to a motion I would second it, and if I could not get one he would second it. Over the week end I have been going over that committee transcript, and through you I am reminding the Minister of National Defence of the frustrations we had when we sat on that committee. If you asked a pertinent question-not an impertinent question but a pertinent question- of the military witnesses, what was your reply seven times out of ten? "That is policy; ask that question of the minister". So we got the minister in front of us and the hon. member for Trinity and myself would put our questions to the minister of national defence.
We asked the same pertinent questions in order to understand defence policy and defence expenditures. Seven times out of ten what was the answer of the minister of national defence? We received a quizzical smile and the answer, "For security reasons those questions cannot be answered", or, "No comment", or, "To answer that question is not in the public interest". I am certain that I do not have to warn the hon. member for Trinity who is now the Minister of National Defence. That was it right down the line. We hope, sir, that is not going to be the experience in the proposed committee, but I am very sorry to say I am afraid it is going to be unless there is a change in the attitude of the Minister of National Defence.
Don't prejudge.

He wonders why I say that. It is because of the way he answers, evades and weasels on questions asked on orders of the day. If that is going to be his attitude in the committee, it will be as big a failure as the one in 1960. I sincerely hope this will not be the case.
In all my life in parliament, sir-and that is a long time now-I have never threatened. However I do want to say this as an intimation to the minister, that I anticipate being a member of this committee when it is established, and having sat with the now Minister of National Defence on the committee in 1960 when he was a member of the opposition, let him not be surprised-because basically the picture has not changed-if I ask

Appointment of Defence Committee him the identical questions which he asked of the three Conservative ministers of national defence and expect the answers that he did not get and fumed because he could not get them. I will not only speak from memory, sir; I will also speak with the book right alongside me.
I notice that the resolution says the terms of reference of this committee will include moving from place to place. That is interesting. I think that provision should be there, but I would not be too concerned about the committee moving from place to place. The information required can be obtained right here in the city of Ottawa from the Minister of National Defence and the members of his department, if they want to give it to the committee. I can assure the house that moving from place to place is not too important. The other day the minister mentioned that he had had the opportunity of moving around and visiting military camps. He is not the only one; there are other hon. members in this House of Commons who over the years have had the opportunity to move around. There are quite a few of us. I was one of the fortunate ones to have the experience in 1961 of being a member of the official delegation from this House of Commons and visiting, I think, every Canadian camp in France and Germany and the majority of the official headquarters of the United States.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence has time after time called these visits briefings. They are not briefings; they are an attempt at brainwashing. I have visited the majority of our military camps and have attended every so-called briefing, and a briefing is an attempt at brass brainwashing. Not only that, but as the committee moves around on these "briefings" they will encounter the same experience that the Minister of National Defence and myself encountered in the House of Commons committee; that is, evasion and weaseling. I can remember when we were in Soest and Zweibriicken and all through there that if on the briefings we asked a really pertinent question about Canada's role in defence we were told, "Sorry, sir; perhaps you had better ask that question of the next highest echelon", and when we got to the next highest echelon and put the question the answer was, "Sorry, sir; I think perhaps you ought to ask that of SACEUR or the next highest echelon". I followed that through from Soest to Zweibriicken until our five days in Paris at the NATO parliamentary conference, when I had an opportunity to ask the highest echelon, and what was the answer, "Sorry, sir; for security reasons we cannot answer that question".
What did you ask for, Harold?

The problem was that I knew the questions to ask and the things we wanted to know, but they were not prepared to answer. That has been my experience in five years both on the defence committee and in travelling around as a member of the Canadian delegation to the NATO parliamentary conference in Paris and visiting our stations in Germany and France.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of National Defence have asked for our co-operation. They will certainly get it. All we ask in return is the co-operation of the Minister of National Defence. All we ask is his confidence. We hope the information we seek can be given in public, but if it cannot, then give it in camera.
I can assure the Minister of National Defence that when I was leader of the opposition in British Columbia in the last war and questions were asked of the G.O.C. western command, the premier and myself knew from week to week the inner secrets of western command. That was the only time I think my own colleagues ever hated me, because I would not tell them whereof I knew. We worked that way.
This committee is as far as possible entitled to know the defence policy of Canada and its needs and requirements so that Canada may participate in the best possible way in the maintenance of peace and the maintenance and extension of democratic principles throughout the world. Mr. Speaker, we look forward to the establishment of this committee. We hope that the words we have heard thus far from the Minister of National Defence will be carried into effect and that as far as is humanly, governmentally and politically possible within the ultimate realm of security, he will take this committee into his confidence. We hope that, irrespective of what the committee recommends, it will have the full consideration of his department and of the government.
As I have said, sir, I only want the experience of sitting on this committee and being able to ask questions on government policy in defence matters, but I would like to add only one thing on the question of policy. You will understand, Mr. Speaker, why it came to my mind. Yesterday the Pope died in Rome. There are three days of mourning in Italy and nine days for the five hundred million Catholics throughout the world. Last night the leaders of the world expressed their regrets at his death and said many things about his ideology and his principles. Last night

at eleven o'clock I watched the C.B.C. television news and I heard the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and what he had to say about the late Pope, about his goals and objectives, his principles and his efforts in working for peace. After hearing what the Prime Minister had to say about the late Pope John XXIII I heard what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had to say about the late Pope and his efforts for peace.
I want to ask the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition whether what they said on television last night does not make them liars so far as defence and foreign policy are concerned in view of the attributes which they applied to the man who died yesterday in Rome. What did that man say which was so highly praised by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition on the eleven o'clock C.B.C. television news last night? What did the man they were talking about say? Do I need to remind them? The title of the encyclical letter is "Pacem in Terris", papal documents series No. 7,4,1963, item No. 63,8. I read from page 23 of this encyclical letter issued at Rome on April 11, 1963:
The production of arms is allegedly justified on the grounds that in present day conditions peace cannot be preserved without an equal balance of armaments. And so, if one country increases its armaments, others feel the need to do the same; and if one country is equipped with nuclear weapons, other countries must produce their own, equally destructive.
Consequently, people live in constant fear lest the storm that every moment threatens should break upon them with dreadful violence. And with good reason, for the arms of war are ready at hand. Even though it is difficult to believe that anyone would deliberately take the responsibility for the appalling destruction and sorrow that war would bring in its train, it cannot be denied that the conflagration may be set off by some uncontrollable and unexpected chance. And one must bear in mind that, even though the monstrous power of modern weapons acts as a deterrent, it is to be feared that the mere continuance of nuclear tests, undertaken with war in mind, will have fatal consequences for life on the earth.
Justice, then, right reason and humanity urgently demand that the arms race should cease; that the stockpiles which exist in various countries should be reduced equally and simultaneously by the parties concerned; that nuclear weapons should be banned; and that a general agreement should eventually be reached about progressive disarmament and an effective method of control. In the words of Pius XII, our predecessor of happy memory:
"The calamity of a world war, with the economic and social ruin and the moral excesses and dissolution that accompany it, must not be permitted to envelop the human race for a third time."
In view of the statement of the Prime Minister on the C.B.C. news last night, the almost adoring attributes he expressed with regard to the works and ideology of Pope John and in view of the similar expressions of the Leader of the Opposition, I can only

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this first opportunity to congratulate the Speaker on his election to that office and to congratulate you, sir, on your election as Deputy Speaker. Discussion on this motion to set up a defence committee has revealed considerable difference of opinion as to the functions of the committee, how it will be carried on and what it will accomplish. The speeches of the leaders of the Social Credit and New Democratic parties indicated that they look to the committee to be a body to determine defence policy, and I presume that assumption on their part is only natural in view of the demands made by the former leader of the opposition during the past two years and particularly because of the statements he made during the election campaign in connection with this matter.
However, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made his opening statement I think he indicated a considerable shift in his position from that which he had taken when he was on this side of the house. He indicated that his interpretation of the terms of reference was that the committee would be able to discuss defence policy and would be able to make recommendations if it so wished but the determination of policy would remain with the government, as indeed I think it must under our system of responsible government. Under these circumstances I doubt very much whether the way in which the committee will carry on and the type of discussion that will take place will be very much different from that which took place in the committees of 1958 and 1960 when there was a great deal of discussion on policy matters although the committees were set up to examine defence expenditures. However, when you are discussing defence expenditures you inevitably get into the field of policy because all such expenditures are related to the types of equipment being secured, what they are going to be used for and things of that kind.
I believe that this committee can serve a useful purpose in informing its members, members of the house and the general public with regard to the organization, equipment and capabilities of our defence forces, the problems in defence and the policies being followed. I hope there will be a good deal of information given and a good deal of discussion on all of those matters.

Appointment of Defence Committee
I do not believe, however, that it can be an effective body so far as policy-making is concerned. One of the basic reasons for this was touched upon by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who spoke just a moment ago. He complained that a large number of the questions he asked during his visit to Europe and to other places had not been answered on the grounds of security. In so far as defence is concerned, security requirements, particularly our responsibilities to our allies in NATO in regard to security, make it impossible to put before a committee of this kind all the information on which defence policy is based and must be based.
I have heard it suggested at various times that all information, could be given to a committee of this kind in secret session. However, I must say that experience over the past 18 years has shown me, and I think has shown everyone who has been here for a long time, that such information generally appears in the newspapers within 24 hours after it has been given to the committee. Nobody ever knows how this information leaks out, but it does become part of the public domain. I feel this situation makes it impossible to give a committee of this sort all the security information which would be essential to enable it to act in the way that some members who have already spoken think it should act, that is as a policy-making body.
If the committee is to do successfully the job that it can do, there is one essential requisite and that is that members of the committee approach their task with open minds rather than with a set partisan position and the objective of trying to publicize this position to the greatest extent possible. One of the characteristics of most parliamentary committees is that they are political forums, to some extent, and with subjects such as defence and external affairs, the greater the extent to which the committee is used for these purposes, the less useful work it can accomplish. If the members of the committee approach their work with set ideas and spend all their time trying to elicit facts which they believe will support those ideas, and to discredit facts which they think are contrary to those ideas, I doubt whether the committee will be able to accomplish useful work in the way of enlightening the members and the general public.
During the course of the remarks the minister made when he was speaking in this debate, there was one statement to which I must take objection. He complained that he was unable to get any information about defence when he was in opposition. This statement is demonstrably not true. Every question that the minister asked when he was in

opposition, that is written questions, questions on orders of the day or when the estimates of the department were being discussed, was answered. He might not have been satisfied with all the answers. In some cases, the only answer that could be given was that security considerations prevented the question being answered. Nevertheless, he was given all the information it was possible to give him. I can vouch for this fact, so far as I am concerned, and the same thing is true so far as my predecessor was concerned. I take considerable objection to this statement made by the minister last week.
A very large amount of information in regard to defence matters was given to the committees of 1958 and 1960. All anyone has to do in order to determine that fact is to peruse the reports of those committees. He will ascertain that there was discussion of all the weapons which subsequently became the subject of so much general debate and discussion throughout Canada. I must say that I think the difficulty of the minister, when he was in opposition, was that he refused to accept information. In other words, it was a case of the old saw: you can lead a horse to water but you can't make him drink. This was, essentially, the position of the minister. His whole approach, during the time he was in opposition, was to denigrate everything that was done in connection with defence. According to him, no single piece of equipment we secured was right. We should not have had it, we should have obtained something else. Nothing that was done in connection with defence, no policy that was followed, was correct. Something else should have been done. In other words, his whole purpose at that time was not to get information, not to try to see that Canada had the best defence effort possible, but merely to belabour the government for political purposes. I will say that in opposition he was the perfect example of the attitude which would make this committee unworkable or make its work abortive. He was the perfect example of the attitude which I said I hoped would not prevail amongst the members of the committee. I hope that they will approach the task with open minds and be prepared to examine the facts in an impartial manner.
I trust that in so far as this committee is concerned the government will not follow the tactics that they used in connection with the defence committees of 1951, 1952 and 1953. I was a member of those committees. At that time, there was a great mass of detail presented to the committee, largely irrelevant so far as the real issues were concerned. The result was that the committee was bogged down in these details and it was unable to

get around to the consideration of the important matters which it should have been considering. I believe the Liberals of the day thought these tactics were very clever. I trust there will be no repetition of that sort of thing. I mention this particularly because there seemed to be some hint of these tactics in the minister's speech when he talked about the need to put vast amounts of information before the committee, to take trips here and there, and so on. If this is the method followed in carrying out the work of the committee,
I can readily see that the committee will degenerate into the same sort of operation that was so unsuccessful in 1951, 1952 and 1953.
I hope that will not be done.
A good deal of time has been spent during this debate in a discussion of defence policy. My position in that regard, especially in relation to nuclear weapons, I think is sufficiently well known to the members of this house and to the country generally that I need not take up the time of the house by reviewing it. I would, however, like to say this: During the Conservative period in office we followed a policy of fully supporting NATO, NORAD and the United Nations, and of contributing to them the men and equipment required to meet our fair share of the collective responsibility of maintaining peace and the security of the western world. This involved the acquisition of four weapons systems which are effective only when they are armed with nuclear warheads. The final step of securing these warheads was the one step which was not taken at that time.
At the present time, the Liberals have adopted this policy in its entirety, so far as one can see. I believe that they should be honest and say that they have adopted the Conservative defence policies of the last five years instead of trying to pin their position to the narrow ground of merely living up to commitments made by the previous government.
The result of the government's failure to state frankly it now believes the Conservative government's policy was a wise one is further confusion, and we have the Gilbert and Sullivan, or perhaps Alice in Wonderland situation, of Liberal spokesmen defending the Conservative policy of the past five years, and some Conservative spokesmen attacking it. I trust one of the things this committee may be able to do is clear up the general confusion in regard to defence policy, and where the various parties stand on that very important matter.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Certainly.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that the acquisition of these four weapons systems indicated an intention on the part of the government to supply them the ammunition which would make them effective.

Mr. Speaker,
this is not the first time I have stood up in this house and spoken on defence, and in order that the gentlemen of the fourth estate may not be misled any further I would like to make my own personal position clear. It was stated in the Montreal Gazette of May 24 that I supported the N.D.P. motion. The N.D.P. motion, on the face of it, was to the effect that we should not have nuclear arms in Canada. That is not why I supported it. The reason was because it was interpreted by our side that the Liberal party purported to complete an agreement with the United States with regard to acquiring nuclear warheads for Canadian forces, and on Canadian soil, without full consultation with parliament. That was the reason why I voted in favour of the N.D.P. motion, as a vote of censure.
I want to make sure that Canadian sovereignty is secured in any agreement we make with any country. Personally I am against nuclear war, like everybody else within earshot of me and like everyone else in the world. But, Mr. Speaker, we live in the twentieth century. We live in the era of nuclear warheads, and I fully believe that only the deterrent power of the United States has prevented Russia from imposing her will on the western world. This is not to say I am willing to accept nuclear arms and nuclear warheads holus-bolus, on Canadian soil.
I made my position clear on September 12, 1961, when I spoke on this question in the house, and I will not bore you by repeating it. On May 23 this year I reiterated my stand. Briefly, what I am asking is that we take the full moral commitment of supporting our United States allies. Then, if we take that full moral commitment, the question of the distribution of weapons is only incidental.
I am ready to put my life and my talents, such as they are, at the disposal of the western world under the leadership of the United States in the military sphere, but if I make such a commitment I would like a reciprocal commitment on the part of my United States allies to always recognize Canada as a sovereign nation. The fact that they are larger than we makes no difference. If we had a population of 185 million people

Appointment of Defence Committee would the United States expect to locate atomic weapons on our soil without a proper two way commitment?
We should face the moral issue properly and decide we are with the United States in resisting communist aggression on this planet. Once we decide to do that, the details are not very important, and we should stop playing politics on this point on both sides of the border.
If the government through this committee, is going to show the Canadian people what our attitude is to joint defence then we will get somewhere, but if this committee is just going to be a way of passing the buck, and smothering us with a lot of straw and no wheat, then I would be opposed to establishing a committee because it will have a bad effect on public opinion and on our position in the eyes of the whole world. However, if the committee achieves this, then I would like to be on the committee and discuss the matter fully with hon. members of the Liberal party.
It is not the responsibility of the opposition to set government policy. As I see it, we have just had an election on this very issue. We were turned out of office because it was said in the press, on the radio and television, that we did not have the courage to determine a policy and negotiate a working agreement with our allies. That, Mr. Speaker, is not so. I have just heard the former minister of national defence say he had this clearcut policy, but never in public or private did he say he was dickering with the Americans for a policy that was acceptable. There may be reasons for this, and I think he gave one in the Calgary Herald, some 18 months ago.
I hold in my hand a paper put out by the Calgary Herald which, on the last page, states that the former minister commended a series of articles on defence published in the Herald and suggested that they should be given the widest possible circulation. The punch line in this paper can be summed up in one short paragraph:
On the other hand, all the nuclear weapons are in American hands, and American law requires that they be used only upon order of the United States government.
This is not a bilateral affair; it is only on the order of the United States government that they can be used. The paragraph continues:
There are tricky questions of sovereignty to be decided here, and they can probably be decided only by agreement (secret if necessary) between the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States.
How can a committee discuss what can only be discussed between the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of

Canada? I have to put my faith somewhere.
I put it squarely in our democratic way of solving the question. Having pooled our resources and opinions and having picked out the best man we can find by public consent, now I am willing to put this responsibility for a secret agreement-and I think a secret agreement is necessary-fully upon the shoulders of the Prime Minister of this country. Let him work out the secret agreement. Let him come up with the decisive action for which the Canadian public is looking. Let us have no more talk about committees or the joint action of four parties. Frankly I do not trust the joint action of four parties.

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business.

Mr. Speaker, as to Bill C-3 the purpose of which is to change the name of the district of Charlevoix to that of Charlevoix-Montmorency, as it has been announced, may I be permitted to put forward my personal opinion on that question; and I have no doubt that a good number of residents in my native riding of Quebec-Montmorency have the same opinion. (Text):
Mr. Speaker, in order, also, to pay a tribute to your very practical bilingualism which will surely facilitate our mutual understanding in this distinguished chamber, an understanding which is so dear to the leaders of the present government and to their colleagues, allow me to extend to you my warmest congratulations upon your welcome nomination to this most important post in our country's administration, as many other hon. members have done before me.
To come back, now, to the second reading of Bill C-3, an act to amend the Representation Act regarding the electoral district of Charlevoix, may I continue in French, my native tongue, which is naturally much more familiar to me?
(Translation):
I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that at first the principle of this bill seemed to me good and even desirable. However, after having given the matter some thought, I now wonder if this change would not lead to some confusion, as we already have the well-known constituency of Quebec-Montmorency.
I wish to state here that I always had a soft spot for Montmorency, as I was born in Ville Montmorency, and I return there regularly to visit my numerous relations. My ancestors came from Baie St. Paul, in Charlevoix county, while by a remarkable coincidence, the hon. member for that constituency was born in Montmagny-L'Islet, which I have the honour to represent in this house. That being so, I sincerely hope that my hon. friend will understand and forgive if I take a special interest in his bill.

I would remind you, Mr, Speaker, that, as you probably already know, it is not the first time that Charlevoix's designation has been changed. The hon. member said so himself a moment ago. Our distinguished fellow member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) will perhaps be surprised to know that what is now the county of Charlevoix was, at first, part of the county of Northumberland, when it was created in 1792.
In 1829, Northumberland was divided in two counties, Montmorency and Saguenay, the latter's limits comprising what is now the county of Charlevoix, which is the subject matter of this debate.
In 1858, the eastern part of the county of Saguenay became a separate county and was called Charlevoix, after Pierre Francois Xavier Charlevoix, a Jesuit father who wrote a history of New France which was published in Paris in 1744 and was a great success.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I am now thinking of my fellow members who are dedicated fishermen even if they would rather stress the social angle-I am happy to point out that this mountainous county with many picturesque sites, where three rivers flow into the St. Lawrence, is a paradise for fishermen. I might mention the Gouffre river, at Baie St. Paul, the Malbaie, at La Malbaie, and the Noire river, at St. Simeon, where the catch can be marvellous.
But to go on with my remarks, history tells us that like an easily comforted widower, Charlevoix was unable to live alone. That is how it came about that, in 1917, it was united with the county of Montmorency and, in 1926, with the county of Saguenay. I do not know exactly if this was due to household or other troubles, but those unions were not lasting ones. There was a divorce, or rather a separation because of an ever increasing family- which would be more acceptable- and Charlevoix again for the last few years has been on its own and apparently finds this rather tedious.
I therefore can very well understand, as you probably can, Mr. Speaker, why the present incumbent of this county is so gentle, to whom his voters apparently complained about this widowhood which I shall call "districo-electoral". For, Mr. Speaker, you know that Charlevoix still has all its charm and is a very acceptable match for Montmorency, as suggested by the hon. member. You just have to refer to the book Dans nos mon-tagnes by Rev. Lionel Boivin, priest of the Assumption parish at Les Eboulements.

Charlevoix has various parishes which were established under the French rule, and all are situated on the northern shore of the St. Lawrence-I might, among others, mention St. Pierre and St. Paul of Baie St. Paul. Those who have been listening to the radio and television programs-I have devoted 13 or 14 years of my life to that field-will recall a very popular person on the radio, Mr. Albert Duquesne, called Alexis, who came from Baie St. Paul. There are also the parishes of St. Francois, Petite-Riviere, Chateau-Richer, Ste Anne de Beaupre and St. Joachim, founded in 1722.
That is interesting history.
On the Montmorency side, we might perhaps recall that since the redistribution in 1924, the former Quebec county has become Quebec-Montmorency, as it is known today.
That is another excellent match. It is named after the Montmorency falls, so called by Champlain in 1630-this is going back quite a bit-to honour the duke of Montmorency, third viceroy of New France. Those falls are 240 feet high, which is 75 feet higher than Niagara falls, and I do not say this to spite our colleagues from Ontario. Mr. Speaker, the mention of the height of the Montmorency falls may explain why we perhaps look down on such a proposal. But we find some gentility in the name of Montmorency, which reminds us of Anne de Montmorency, high constable of France, Henry I, duke of Montmorency and marshal of France, the also quite illustrious Frangois-Xavier de Mont-morency-Laval, the first bishop of Quebec who left his name to an institution of high learning, the Laval University of Quebec city, which I am proud to have attended during my youth.
We could also mention several other names, the Montmorency river which had some importance in politics or international politics since the Montmorency river, as you undoubtedly know, has its source in lake des Neiges, a wonderful place in the national park where prominent people made a fishing trip during an important conference held in Quebec city-if my memory does not fail me-at the Chateau Frontenac where the President of the United States, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, a late prime minister of Canada, and representatives from Russia met and made quite a fishing trip to lake des Neiges.
Therefore, as you see, a lot can be said on the merits and charms of Montmorency.
We do not necessarily see an improper alliance in this case, Mr. Speaker, but, as you undoubtedly know, it is when the bans are published that those who know of some reasons why such marriage should not be made are called upon to come forward as soon as possible. That is why I made those remarks.
To conclude, I wish to point out a serious objection in addition to the multiplicity of the name of Montmorency used for other ridings, it is that this union seems to be between next of kins and I would be most concerned over the brood bom from such a union.
Moreover, to get back to serious things, as the government has the intention to introduce soon a measure concerning a redistribution of our ridings through a special committee that will be instituted for that purpose, I think it would be premature to comply with the request of the hon. member for Charlevoix because, in my opinion, that would not settle in a concrete way the problem which we face at the present time in that field.
That is why I object to this bill; besides, I am sure that the study which will be made through the proposed redistribution would serve to dot the I's and cross the T's; this would be better than putting in commas that might put us in an unfortunate situation.
It only remains for me to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for listening to me so patiently and I hope that my next contribution will be of interest to all the members of this house.

to study the redistribution of electoral districts, that is the revision of the Representation Act, I am of the opinion that bills which run counter to measures already advocated in the speech from the throne are surely premature. To my way of thinking, that is reason enough to reject measures such as the one now before us, because the matter concerns but one constituency and not all the country's electoral districts.
Mr. Chairman, it is rather strange to see the results sometimes brought about by changes in the names of certain districts. I do not doubt the good intentions of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger); indeed, as he said himself, one quarter of the population of the federal riding of Charlevoix live within the boundaries of the provincial constituency of Montmorency and three quarters in the constituency of Charlevoix.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency told us that three quarters of Montmorency riding, which are located in my constituency, should be called Montmorency. I must say that I agree in principle with the single name for a single constituency.
The name of Charlevoix is a very nice name with its history, as it has been said so eloquently a few moments ago.
The name of Montmorency is also an historical name; it has also a beautiful history attached to it that would deserve a constituency all to itself.
Sometimes it may be just a whim to ask for a change of name. This afternoon, I had the time to make a quick list of the names which have been changed in various ridings since the last redistribution of seats, which dates back to 1952.
If we consider chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, we note that the lawmakers passed legislation of a general nature when proceeding with the 1952 redistribution. If we go back farther than 1958, we note that in 1953 and 1954, as evidenced by chapter 32, they had to give a double-barrelled name to ridings.
At this time, I think of the Speaker of this house and of the second assistant Clerk who have to recognize the members not only by name but also by the name of their ridings, which is an enormous task.

That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 24 members to be designated by the house at a later date.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
At five o'clock I had just indicated that I would have no faith in a defence policy which was a combined policy of the four groups in this house. I suggested, and I still think so, having thought it over again during the supper recess, that responsibility for defence policy under our parliamentary system must rest squarely on the shoulders of the government. The Canadian people have made a somewhat shaky decision as to whom they expect to make this policy, but having accepted office the Liberal party is, in my view, solidly seized with these responsibilities. If we do set up this committee it will never be more than a fact finding committee and we cannot expect it to make decisions of the kind to which I have referred.
In recent months we have heard talk about anti-Americanism. I do not think any party in this house is anti-American. Far from it. I think it is high time we stopped any such talk and got down to seeing just how far we can co-operate with the United States. In my opinion this co-operation must be 100 per cent. Many of us feel that our budget expenditures on defence are much too high. However, I cannot agree with this view. Expenditure in the United States on defence is at a much higher per capita than ours. Moreover, their attitude toward national service is more realistic than ours and I, for one, would like to see national defence discussed in this committee. I think it is high time the people of Canada looked at the twentieth century and its challenges, forgetting old mistakes and recriminations, and decided we must have arrangements in keeping with modern needs. If we are to match the United States in per capita dollars spent on our defence, I think we should also match them according to our population, in manpower. We cannot do this unless our young men and women are given the chance to be prepared, physically and mentally, for the challenges which I am sure will lie ahead for many years to come.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten) .1
The Calgary Herald, in that article which it put out some 18 months ago to which I have already referred, faced these problems clearly, particularly with regard to expenditure, and if the house will bear with me I will quote a paragraph or so from that article which I think is relevant to the issue before us.
Canadians can scarcely argue at this point that defence constitutes an insupportable burden on their pocketbooks. As a matter of cold fact, defence expenditures have scarcely squeezed the pockets of most of us at all.
Furthermore, since the survival of this and other free nations may depend entirely on adequate defence arrangements, it is impossible to say that such and such a level of defence expenditure is "too high" if it isn't adequate to do the job it is intended to do.
If we value our sovereignty and our nationhood, we ought to be prepared to spend whatever is necessary, even at the cost of some sacrifice, to defend our country. No matter how much we spend, if we spend one dollar less than is necessary to do the job adequately, we shall have spent too little.
This is not to argue for lavish and needless expenditures on defence luxuries. It is merely to state that once the best brains we can hire have decided on what the job is, and the minimum weaponry necessary to do it, then Canadians, as a matter of pride, ought to be prepared to spend the money to acquire such weaponry.
This brings me to the question: are our present weapons adequate for defence. Perhaps they are not. But I think we have done our best. When the Arrow program was cancelled-and this was one of the decisions which the former government made; I think it was a proper decision-we looked around for some other form of defence against the bomber. We built the CF-104 for the reconnaissance role and we purchased 66 Voodoo planes from the United States to replace the Arrow as a defensive weapon against manned bombers. We were severely criticized by all parties in the opposition for doing this but I say, today, that we would not be able to accept the commitment we expect to have presented to us in the near future unless we had taken this step to prepare our country. As far as the Arrow is concerned, I understand the United States refused to include it in their defence program. I am most unhappy, most depressed, with the thought that considerations of defence go beyond what our defence planners say is our goal to deter the aggressor, and that once they have passed the point that any logical, sane person knows is sufficient, they go on thinking in terms of world war I and world war II-strategic concepts; consideration of bases; the military advantage of one side or the other; who has got the most of which sort of weapons, and who has the supremacy in this line or that. I suggest there is already in the hands of our American allies more than enough deterrent power, and that what we would be doing if we accepted nuclear arms would not be adding to that at all. It is merely taking control of a small part of what we already have. I fail to see how anyone can say this adds to our defence.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate this evening I should first of all like to disclaim any pretentions to being a military expert. I am sure this will be received with great gratitude by our so very knowledgeable Minister of National Defence-that I make no pretensions on this score at all. In the course of a rather chequered military career the most exalted rank I attained was that of corporal, although I must say I attained it more than once, my military career having a certain yo-yo characteristic. But even had I by some miracle attained the rank of field marshal in that very ancient world war in which I took part, I would not be capable of being a military expert in the lunatic world of kilotons, megatons, overkill, first strike and second strike.
So, I have to rely on the views of people who are presumed to be experts, both scientists and military logicians, and I find like most experts they spend a very large amount of their time contradicting each other with great virulence, but there is one thing they all agree on, in fact there is no disagreement at all among accepted military experts and accepted scientists throughout the world on the fact that there is literally no defence against modern weapons of war.
I have an idea that a great deal of our trouble and confusion in Canada today is due to our misuse of words, that we will persist

in using the word "defence" when every authority who has the right to an opinion tells us there is no such thing. In fact it was the general acceptance of that idea that caused the evolution of the theory of the massive deterrent, brought forward by the late unlamented John Foster Dulles. If this theory is valid, Mr. Speaker, and it may very well be valid, it must include an anterior theory, a theory that must be held both by those in control of the western strategy and those in control of the communist strategy, and that theory, conviction and assumption must be on the part of the western world that the Kremlin is inhabited by certifiable lunatics, and on the part of the Russians that the American administration is similarly staffed by lunatics, because let us examine for a moment what are the implications of this theory of the massive deterrent.
It is that while there is no means of defending ourselves in the traditional sense of the word from destruction, complete and near destruction, it may still be possible to frighten any prospective enemy from attacking us first, by waving in his face the ability to strike him even more severely than he has struck us.
Now, as I say, this theory depends on the assumption that each side must consider the other to be composed of lunatics. After all, only a lunatic in the Pentagon could imagine that any benefits would occur to the American people by creating a radioactive desert in central Asia and Europe-yet it is on this basis that the Russians operate today in building up their deterrents; it is their presumption, evidently, that the Americans are lunatic enough to embark on the projects which could be of no possible benefit to them after it had been completed. And, in a similar way, the Americans must hold the same view with regard to the Russians and consider that the Russians could seriously envisage creating a radioactive desert in North America which could be of no conceivable benefit to them or anyone else.
If this theory of massive deterrence is valid,
