Now I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the theory of massive deterrence is valid- and it is the only theory of defence in the world today; the only theory which is accepted by military and scientific authorities-then, surely, this deterrence is already as large as is necessary for any eventuality. It seems to me that if this tremendous volume of these deterrent weapons is not enough to frighten a potential enemy, any contribution Canada could make would be derisory in its nature, so minute would it be.
While reading Mr. McNamara's statement published, as I say, in Science magazine, the thought occurred to me that in making public these facts in a somewhat astonishing manner, followed by his assistant making public equally remarkable facts, the authors of these statements were attempting to come to grips with that military and industrial complex against which President Eisenhower warned the American people in the last few months of his term of office. We may well not be strengthening the hands of those in the United States who are seeking to curb this headlong drive to catastrophe which Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Appointment of Defence Committee McNamara speaks of when we meekly accept further weapons, meekly accept a role in this devastating and lunatic business.
I have been interested and somewhat dismayed on hearing statements made by the present Prime Minister both before he was prime minister and since he assumed that office-statements indicating that in his opinion Canada's national honour was involved in this question of acquiring nuclear weapons for which, demonstrably, there is no possible need or use. It struck me at the time when he spoke in this vein in the House of Commons that this was a most curious concept of national honour, a most curious concept indeed, namely, that we were bound by a lunatic agreement-if there was such an agreement-to spend our treasure and our resources, to the exclusion of much more useful activities, not on adding to western strength but merely going through the motions in an absurd and ridiculous manner so as to pretend we have a role to play in the military world of today. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is looking for stains on our national honour he had better not look in this direction-in the direction of unfulfilled, ridiculous pledges. He had better look at the unemployment, at the slums, at the lack of a medical insurance plan, at the difficulties we are experiencing in education, at the foreign ownership of most of our country. These are the things this government should be attending to.
Even if one agrees with this argument- and I fail to see how one could disagree- the question may be asked: why does the United States press us along this course, and press us to a most striking degree. I would suggest there are two possible reasons. One is a matter of prestige. There is, on the other side of the world, another complex of nations, communist nations. Largely for reasons of prestige the Soviet union decided not to release the east European countries which are under her domination. Although they constitute a continual worry and threat to her, it would be a severe blow to national prestige if they slipped outside the Soviet orbit. I suggest some similar sort of considerations may well be operating in the minds of those in the Pentagon in Washington who are already in control of sufficient nuclear power to destroy the world several times over. There is no other logical reason, unless one takes another possibility, one which I would hope is not the right one, and that is that we are being pressed today so that Canada may be a protecting area, a cordon sanitaire if you like, for the nuclear weapons aimed at the United States. After all, I suppose the first responsibility of any government is, if it is at all possible to do so, to deflect any attack upon its own people and its own
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
territory on to any other territory. One might take that position, and if it is one of the motives of the United States, the government of that country is merely doing its duty.
I should like to examine this proposition in regard to this question of nuclear armaments and defence measures in toto, and to examine the possibilities and the probabilities in the world with a view to assessing our behaviour and that of our possible adversaries. It is a well known psychological fact that people who insist on attempting to guard against every possible danger or mishap very rapidly become mentally unhinged. The sane person is the one who guards against probabilities; he does not waste his efforts, anxieties and worries in trying to cover every possible contingency. In fact the people who do so find their way into our mental homes. A very well known mental disturbance is that of the person who suffers from a "compulsive cleanliness" because he is always afraid that some kind of germ will get on his hands and cause his illness or death, and who spends his time frantically washing his hands and disinfecting them, and who eventually lands in the "loony bin". It may be possible that he will get a germ on his hands and by a million to one chance it does kill him, but no sane person operates on that basis. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that right now we are faced with mass lunacy in centres of power in the world. I suggest that those in control of the military power in the world today are attempting to protect themselves not merely against what is probable or likely but against what might possibly, by some strange concatenation of events, take place, and the result of their insanity is that it has brought the world almost to the brink of disaster.
Now, the question may well be asked: Is there a useful role for Canada to play in the world today in this regard? I suggest to you, sir, that there is an extremely useful role. I want to illustrate that role by referring to some events which took place last October. Those of us here who were members of the twenty fifth parliament will recall that evening in October when the prime minister of Canada rose to tell us that the President of the United States had informed him about half an hour earlier that the United States fleet was deployed in the Caribbean blockading Cuba; that any ship approaching Cuba would be stopped and searched; that any ship refusing to stop would be sunk; that any retaliation in any part of the world would result in the outbreak of a thermo-nuclear war. I do not need to remind hon. members of that dramatic and nerve-wracking period here in the House of Commons and throughout the world.

Now, Mr. Speaker, when people examine the Cuban crisis I note that they have a tendency to go only half way back in the chain of events which led us to this precipice. Most of them go back no further than the misguided effort or pretense-whichever it was- of Mr. Khrushchev to put missile bases in Cuba. Most people go no further back than that. It is, to their minds, what created the crisis. Others who are a little more perceptive go a little further back as far as the Cuban revolution which brought Fidel Castro to power. This was the start of the chain of events which led us last October to the brink of thermonuclear destruction. But I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that we must go further back than that to find the real reason why the world was perched last October on the brink of disaster-back far beyond the Castro revolution. We must go back to the condition in which Cuban people were living for generations before the Castro revolution.
I have no means of knowing what conditions are like in Cuba today. I have not been there and one gets conflicting reports. But I and other hon. members of the house know that before the Castro revolution the people of Cuba were living in unbelievable misery, squalor and terror under the Batista regime, and predecessors of a similar nature. And we know something else-that not one of us lifted one finger to help the Cuban people out of their appalling misery. We took it for granted that that was the way the Latin Americans lived. We said: "It's too bad they don't understand our democratic procedures. It's too bad they are not as developed as we are". We never lifted a finger to help them, yet we knew what was going on in Cuba. Our Department of External Affairs knew because they had steady reports coming in.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that when we are seeking for a valid and viable role for Canada to play in the world today that bitter lesson should be borne in mind. Because there are today throughout the world many Cubas in which the people are living in the squalor, misery and terror in which the Cuban people lived not very long ago.

It is for that reason, sir, that I have dwelt on this question of an alternative role because I consider that to be the only valid defence role in the world today.
Now, sir, perhaps you will permit me, just for the few moments I have at my disposal, to deal with one specific aspect of defence. I refer to the question of nuclear arms. I have dealt with this on a tactical basis and I should now like to say a word or two, with your permission, on the moral question involved. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people cannot afford to dodge this moral issue.
There has been throughout the last few decades a steady escalation of horror in the prosecution of war. I referred, when I began my speech, to my own experiences of war, a very primitive war and one which had more in common with the middle ages than this lunatic world in which we live today. But I also recall during the last war the horror that descended on the world when the first news of mass bombings came to our knowledge, and how those outraged protests died away and people finally accepted the idea that to destroy civilian populations as a deliberate military project was acceptable in this strange world in which we live.
That was bad enough when we were only destroying people of that generation, when we were only knocking down the material bases

You have asked us, Mr. Speaker, to restrict ourselves in this debate to talking about the committee that is to be appointed. I was also glad to learn that the number of members on the committee has been increased from 18 to 24, because that will give the opposition more opportunity to make their views known. That is what we need in regard to this question of defence.
I am very pleased to see that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has decided to allow discussions of defence policy in this committee and I will be more pleased when I see it added officially to the resolution, because sometimes just making the remark in the house does not mean it is carried out.

I wonder, though, exactly how much good such a committee will be. Will the government pay any attention to the recommendations of the committee? Will they listen to its recommendations on policy? I am very sure they will not. I say this because I was a soldier, and I really cannot see how the government can have its policy set by a committee composed of members of all parties. It is a good out for them, but I do not think they will take it.
I also wonder, Mr Speaker, whether the government is going to pay attention to the committee should it, say, recommend that we do not have nuclear arms in Canada, that we do not equip our out of date Bomarcs with nuclear warheads, because our Bomarcs at this late date are not the last word in defence against nuclear bombers. They are not even as effective as they were five years ago when the idea originated of using Bomarcs in our defence. In addition, with regard to the F-lOl's being equipped with nuclear weapons, they may not be too effective now for the simple reason that they are not as fast an aircraft as would be a fighter plane coming in to attack this country. They would not be a bit of good against intercontinental ballistic missiles, which would be the main method of attack today. Therefore I say it would be a very good thing should this committee recommend that we do not equip the two Bomarc bases in this country with nuclear warheads and that we do not equip our F-lOl's-that is, the Voodoos-with nuclear warheads.
I was rather intrigued in reading what the Minister of National Defence is reported as having said, that it would take four months to train our forces to use nuclear weapons. Does he not know that in the first world war men like Bishop, Barker, Collishaw and McCall, whom I knew so well, went into action with less than five hours training? If this government is going to take four months to train them to use nuclear weapons, what is the matter with the outlook of the Minister of National Defence, who apparently does not know that Canadian fighting men have no peers anywhere in the world. Canadian sailors, soldiers and airmen are at the top of the heap and have always been since Canada became a nation. This has been proved many times. They do not take forever to be trained, and should it be necessary to have them trained quickly I would venture the opinion that they could have these weapons put into their hands and could use them immediately because they are all trained to do the job with conventional weapons and they are trained to do it well.

I want to say that the equipping of NATO with nuclear weapons is a different proposition because NATO is under a different command. It is not located in Canada but on foreign soil. I do want to say that I hope when the committee is set up it will have the powers it is supposed to have and that its recommendations will be listened to. I doubt that very much, of course, but I hope that is the case. I know that the committee will be set up because almost everyone here is in favour of it. Therefore I hope it will be effective and will be listened to.

But if the committee are going to do a real job in the light of what they believe to be the purpose of this committee, then those restrictions must be removed. We have to make a complete departure, not a halfhearted departure as is proposed.
There is something more I should like to mention which I do not believe is inherent at all in the committee set-up and which our friends of the Social Credit party do not understand when they advocate these allparty commons committees. This house is composed of parties, and the representation on these committees is based on the strength of the parties. Now, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made that statement of his in Kingston on March 26, as reported in the press, to the effect that the Liberal party would set up an all-party Commons defence committee right away to take the defence issue away from party politics and so forth, I say, frankly, that was a lot of tripe. That was nothing but pure, unadulterated tripe, because at that time the right hon. gentleman was expecting to win the election, to have a majority. He did not tell the public this, but certainly we, in the House of Commons, know that the composition of committees is according to party strength. If the Liberal party had a majority in this house they would have a majority on that committee.


Then, all that would come out of that committee would be Liberal party resolutions and recommendations. When you say that committees come to conclusions, they come to conclusions on the basis of political muscle. If you have got resolutions to put forward, then you get them passed by means of your voting power. I have had enough experience in the past few years in these various committees to understand just what may happen. Hon. members should remember that there are no minority reports from these committees. There is a majority report that comes back to this house. The government may accept it or may pigeon-hole it. It may do with it as it sees fit because under our parliamentary form of government we do not have government by committee. This is another limitation or restriction on the proposed committee.
It is true that you may have persuasion. I am sure that there are certain eminent journalists who feel that they have as much power of persuasion or influence on the government, and I am not taking anything away from them when I say that, as the conclusions of a committee would have.
Now, I believe there are certain things this committee will want to know once it is set up. First of all, I believe that all the members of the house will want to know the reason for the sudden change in Liberal defence policy which was enunciated on January 12 last. I am sure the decision was arrived at without consultation with the backbenchers on the government side. After all, if we read that booklet-someone has suggested it should be a comic book but perhaps the colours might be wrong-published by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), to which reference has been made on a number of occasions, entitled, "The Liberal Party and its Policy", or something of that nature, we find a very clear, categorical statement of Liberal policy in relation to nuclear arms. Certainly, however, the booklet is not clear on some of the policies enunciated by the present minister when he was opposition defence critic.
I wonder what has happened to the concept of unified command, that sort of overall umbrella? What has happened to that great fleet of mother ships, those transports that were to be built? We remember that famous speech-a lot of hon. members opposite were not here then-that was so widely reported in the press prior to its delivery in the house. This was a great speech on policy. I, of course, felt sorry for the minister's embarrassment at the time, but let us get down to facts. What happened to the policy that was enunciated in that speech? I suppose it has gone into the trash can, like a

lot of other things. This committee will be interested in knowing how the Liberals arrived at this latest policy. After all, so far we have failed to obtain a statement of policy from the hon. gentleman or the associate minister.
We would like very much to hear from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin). There are many problems in his area of responsibility. I am sure he has charge of personnel matters. Are we going to hear from him about our commitments to the United Nations in so far as our armed services are concerned? Are we going to have more personnel who are available for training assignment or policing assignments under the United Nations? Are we going to have more French speaking personnel? The other day it was suggested, I believe, that the Congo would like to have a corps of French speaking Canadian officers as instructors. This situation might also apply to some of the other new African nations. Naturally, this question will affect policy with respect to recruitment.
There is also the question of whether or not recruiting is going to be stepped up in order to bring the forces up to authorized ceilings. Then, how about the balance between the navy, air force and army? I was not there, but I am told that Liberal candidates in the maritimes, certainly in those areas where there are naval stations, played two ends against the middle. They played off the air force against the navy. They said that a Conservative government had neglected the navy. They alienated the navy from the former administration and in other centres they said: down with the navy and up with the air force. We should hear from the associate minister of defence on these matters.
Perhaps the associate minister would also have something to say about the educational policies of the Department of National Defence. Does he consider this would be, within his own province, an unwarranted intrusion into the educational system of the province of Quebec? There are a few other pertinent questions which affect policy. These are points about which this committee would like to hear and about which the house has not heard. I am sure that hon. members, before they decide to establish this committee, would like to have some idea of what it is going to do. After all, if we look at the resolution we find it refers to all those matters pertaining to defence.
In view of the fact that the foreign policy of this country now relates even more closely to national defence policy than it did in the past, are we going to have a declaration
Appointment of Defence Committee from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) as to the policy of this government with respect to those questions involving national defence? Now, Mr. Speaker, I have indicated what I feel are some of the clear restrictions on the efficacy of such a committee. He asked the government to have, prior to the establishment of that committee, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) as well as the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) set forth in this house its defence policy for the future as far as our country is concerned.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that it would be in the interest of all members and, also of the Canadian people, for the government to take its responsibilities and say what it intends to do in the future in respect of each area of national defence. It is all very well to set up a committee, but it should not be restricted, as the hon. member for Edmonton West indicated a while ago, by certain security measures.
I will admit that some problems will be hard to solve on account of the security of our country, but I should not like to see the government take advantage of the situation to keep from the house part of the details concerning our defence policy, so that the Canadian people will also be informed.
It is important that this matter of defence be considered in all its aspects, because the Canadian people want to know every detail.
In my opinion, Canada should not acquire nuclear arms and the estimates of the Department of National Defence should be reduced
tMr. Lambert.]
accordingly. The government should rather concentrate its defence policy on the one field of conventional weapons.
Unfortunately, in the past, particularly under the former Liberal government, we have perhaps been subject to the influence of the United States to an exaggerated degree. We are ready to co-operate with the Americans but, on the other hand, we do not want to become a satellite of the United States. Moreover, we do not want to be dragged into all kinds of expenditures by the American government, when the people of Canada do not have the same financial resources as their southern neighbours.
In that respect, one must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the American government has a budget totalling $100 billion whereas ours amounts to only $6 billion. As a matter of fact, the annual deficit of the Washington government is higher than our whole budget.
In the past, the American government has dragged us into all kinds of expenditures. For instance, we constructed a type of aircraft that became obsolete right after its completion.
I think that the Canadian people are tired of giving their money when it is not used effectively in the field of national defence. That is what we feel is important for the government and that is why we hope that the government will tell us exactly what defence policy it will follow in the future, before we set up that committee.
We do not want Canada to be a satellite of the United States, let alone the servant of Washington. We want sovereignty for Canada. We do not want to be another star, another American state.
Canadians are proud of their sovereignty. They want to co-operate with the Americans, but they do not want to be dominated by them. In brief, we want decisions to be taken only in Ottawa and not in Washington.
At the present time, there is almost no means of defence against intercontinental ballistic missiles, and that applies to the whole world. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that a missile coming from the U.S.S.R. would not take 11J minutes to reach Canada? If we had nuclear weapons in our possession, we who assume the leadership for peace across the world, we would be in a very bad position to tell both great powers-the United States and Russia-to ban nuclear weapons.

Business of the House Mr. Pickersgill: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, if I could answer the question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) I wish to say it is the intention of the government to go on with this debate, which we hope has pretty nearly exhausted itself, and when it has been completed to go ahead with the resolution stage preceding the bill on the economic council. If there was still time tomorrow, although it will be a short day, we would then call the resolution respecting the department of industry. I may have to suggest some change in the order so far as the third item is concerned, on account of engagements of one or two of my colleagues.
